title: Rubio's open call for Cubans to work with the CIA
deck: The US Secretary of State has publicly urged Cubans seeking change to form a 'discrete partnership' with the CIA, turning a long pressure campaign on Havana into an explicit appeal for regime change.

fuel.title: Rubio tells Cubans 'now is the time'
fuel.how: The top US diplomat is openly asking Cubans who want political change to act, which makes regime change a stated aim and not just a hint.

fuel.title: Trump floats warships intervening after Iran
fuel.how: Hours before Rubio spoke, Trump told a rally that warships could intervene on their return from Iran, which puts a military backdrop behind the CIA appeal.

fuel.title: Sanctions policy on Havana in play
fuel.how: The event summary says the appeal could affect US sanctions policy, so economic pressure is likely to move together with the political message.

fuel.title: Migration toward the US put at risk
fuel.how: The event summary says the appeal could affect migration flows toward the United States, since instability or a crackdown in Cuba tends to push people to leave.

card.headline: The US is now openly asking Cubans to work with the CIA to change their government

keyNumber.label: Rubio says 'now is the time', shortly after Trump says warships could intervene on their return from Iran

forYou.line: The US has moved from saying it wants change in Havana to publicly inviting Cubans to help bring it about.
Expect sanctions policy toward Cuba to be a live issue; treat any Cuba exposure as higher risk until the direction is clear.
Naval talk plus possible migration pressure raises the odds of disruptions and tighter enforcement in the Florida Straits (our estimate).
Words are not yet actions. Watch for sanctions moves, naval deployments and Havana's response.

effects.text: Rubio publicly urges Cubans seeking change to form a 'discrete partnership' with the CIA and says 'now is the time'
Trump tells a Friday rally that warships could intervene on their return from Iran, and says Cuba is 'ready to fall'
A covert-cooperation offer made in public is unusual, and it gives Havana a ready propaganda line (our reading)
Havana is likely to tighten internal security and treat contact with US agencies as treason (estimate)
Pressure for new or tougher US sanctions on Cuba may rise, as the event summary suggests
Fear of unrest or a crackdown could raise the number of Cubans trying to leave for the US (estimate)
Governments across Latin America may split over a US regional push that now includes Venezuela and Cuba
Cuba policy may become a bigger issue in US domestic politics ahead of the 3 November midterms (estimate)
If words turn into naval or covert action, the Caribbean could see its sharpest confrontation in decades (low probability)

whatHappened: On 23 October 2026, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Cubans who want political change to form a 'discrete partnership' with the CIA. He told them 'now is the time' to act. Al Jazeera summarised the message as an appeal to work secretly with the CIA to topple their government.
He spoke shortly after President Donald Trump told a Friday rally that warships could intervene in Cuba on their return from Iran, according to The Guardian.
The Trump administration has said repeatedly that it wants a change in Havana's leadership. Euronews notes that Trump himself has said the country is 'ready to fall'.
whyItMatters: Politics: Regime change is no longer implied. The country's top diplomat is saying it in public, and he is addressing ordinary Cubans directly. That raises the stakes for Havana, for the Cubans who might respond, and for any later talks.
Security: Trump's warship remark puts a military shadow behind the CIA appeal. We do not know whether it signals a plan or a pressure tactic. Either way, Havana will have to plan for the worse case.
Sanctions and trade: The event summary says the appeal could affect sanctions policy. Public pressure usually comes with economic pressure, but we have no confirmed new measure yet.
Migration: The summary also flags migration flows toward the US. Cuban history suggests that crises on the island can send people to sea, though nothing in the sources reports a rise yet.

Wider pattern: US forces captured Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro on 3 January 2026, and acting president Delcy Rodriguez now leads under US-backed interim rule. The Cuba appeal and the Venezuela deals do not depend on each other, but both come from one US strategy of pressuring governments it opposes.

winners.why: The administration's stated goal of change in Havana has become official public language.
They get open US backing and attention (though this also brings risk to people inside Cuba).
Not caused by the Cuba appeal, but part of the same US regional push: US licenses cover BP, Chevron, Eni, Maurel & Prom, Repsol and Shell, and exclude China, Russia and Iran.

losers.why: It faces open US calls for its overthrow and a threat of force.
They could face arrest if Havana treats the appeal as proof of subversion (our estimate).

losers.who: Cubans hoping for easier US relations
losers.why: Diplomatic and economic thaw looks less likely while the stated goal is regime change.

whatsNext: Havana's official response and any security measures it announces.
Any new US sanctions or enforcement steps on Cuba.
Where the warships mentioned by Trump actually go.
3 November: US midterm elections, where Trump has been campaigning for candidates.
Signs of movement by sea toward Florida, reported by US or Cuban authorities.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what is the most likely result over the next few months?
options: Pressure campaign continues, with no major military action
A Cuban crackdown triggers a surge of people leaving
US forces or covert action escalate sharply
Talks open between Washington and Havana
predict.explanation: Our base case, about 55%, is that the pressure campaign continues through sanctions, rhetoric and posturing, with no major military action. Escalation is possible, but public threats often exceed what governments actually do. This is author judgement, not a sourced forecast.

timeline.title: Cuban revolution takes power
timeline.detail: Fidel Castro's forces take control. The system they built is the one Washington now wants changed.

timeline.title: Bay of Pigs invasion
timeline.detail: A CIA-backed attempt by Cuban exiles to overthrow Castro fails. It is the best-known US covert effort in Cuba.

timeline.title: US and Cuba announce a thaw
timeline.detail: Presidents Obama and Raul Castro announce moves to restore relations. Later US administrations rolled parts of it back.

timeline.title: Large anti-government protests in Cuba
timeline.detail: Protests across the island were among the biggest in decades. Background from general knowledge; not in the sources.

timeline.title: US forces capture Nicolas Maduro
timeline.detail: Venezuela is then led by acting president Delcy Rodriguez under US-backed interim rule. This is the regional precedent for the Cuba push.

timeline.title: Trump announces a US-Venezuela oil deal
timeline.detail: The deal covers 17 fields. US General License 50C licenses BP, Chevron, Eni, Maurel & Prom, Repsol and Shell and excludes China, Russia and Iran.

timeline.title: Venezuela touts $76bn of oil investment
timeline.detail: Rodriguez says 61 signed agreements (17 with the US) should bring nearly $76bn over five years, with 44 more deals worth about $12bn in talks.

timeline.title: Trump says warships could intervene
timeline.detail: At a Friday rally for candidates, Trump says warships could intervene on their return from Iran, per The Guardian.

timeline.title: Rubio: 'now is the time'
timeline.detail: Moments after Trump's remarks, Rubio urges Cubans seeking change to form a 'discrete partnership' with the CIA.

timeline.title: Appeal reported worldwide
timeline.detail: Euronews and Al Jazeera report the appeal. Euronews notes Trump has claimed Cuba is 'ready to fall'.

causes.name: Long US-Cuba hostility
causes.detail: Since the 1959 revolution the two governments have been adversaries, with covert operations, sanctions and short-lived thaws.

causes.name: Cuban exile politics
causes.detail: Rubio comes from the Cuban-American political world of Florida, which has long pushed for a harder line (background knowledge).

causes.name: Cuba's economic weakness
causes.detail: Years of crisis and shortages are widely reported. This is background knowledge, not from our sources, so treat it as medium confidence.

causes.name: Rally and appeal
causes.detail: Trump's warship remark and Rubio's call came within moments of each other, so they look like one coordinated message.

causes.name: Venezuela precedent
causes.detail: The capture of Maduro and US-backed interim rule show Washington is willing to act against governments it opposes.

causes.name: Stated goal of change in Havana
causes.detail: Euronews notes the administration has repeatedly said it wants a change in Havana's leadership.

causes.name: Domestic politics
causes.detail: Trump was speaking at a rally for candidates, and the midterms are on 3 November (our reading).

stakeholders.name: Marco Rubio
stakeholders.wants: A change of government in Havana
stakeholders.leverage: Diplomacy, sanctions and the public platform of his office
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep the public pressure up and tie it to sanctions and signals to Cubans

stakeholders.name: Donald Trump
stakeholders.wants: A visible win in the region and a strong message at home
stakeholders.leverage: Military options, including the warships he mentioned, and executive sanctions powers
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep claiming Cuba is ready to fall; decide later whether to act

stakeholders.name: Cuban government in Havana
stakeholders.wants: Survival and control of internal security
stakeholders.leverage: Police and security services, nationalist messaging
stakeholders.likelyMove: Denounce US interference and tighten monitoring of dissent (estimate)

stakeholders.name: Cubans seeking change
stakeholders.likelyMove: Mostly caution. Open cooperation with a foreign agency is dangerous

stakeholders.name: The CIA
stakeholders.likelyMove: Silence. Public comment on covert work is unlikely

stakeholders.name: Delcy Rodriguez and Venezuela's interim government
stakeholders.wants: Stability and oil investment under US-backed rule
stakeholders.leverage: Oil: 1.206 million barrels a day in September, up about 30% this year
stakeholders.likelyMove: Continue the US-aligned oil opening and avoid taking Cuba's side

stakeholders.name: Cuban-American voters and politicians
stakeholders.likelyMove: Welcome the appeal and push for sanctions or more

sectors.why: Havana will likely tighten control, but also faces pressure and uncertainty. The net effect is unclear.
The event summary says the appeal could affect sanctions policy. Compliance work on Cuba exposure likely rises.
Warship talk and possible migration push raise naval and coast guard activity (estimate).
Higher tension usually deters visitors and complicates money transfers. Estimate, not sourced.
Separate from the Cuba appeal, but US licenses and deals continue to steer investment to Western firms.
The appeal helps candidates who want a tough line, but other voters may dislike open talk of regime change (our reading).

dailyLife.effect: Rising political risk. Even contact with foreigners could draw attention from state security if Havana tightens controls (estimate).
Sanctions or travel rules could change how money and visits move between the US and Cuba. No measure has been announced.
Greater naval presence and possible migration flows are the main local risks (estimate).
Check government travel advisories. The political climate is more volatile after the appeal.

scenarios.name: Pressure campaign continues
scenarios.looksLike: Rhetoric, new sanctions or enforcement steps and naval posturing, but no invasion or major covert exposure. Havana denounces the US and tightens control.
signposts: New US sanctions or visa rules
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Cuba policy stays a flashpoint in the region and in US domestic politics.

scenarios.name: Crackdown and outflow
scenarios.looksLike: Havana arrests people accused of contact with the CIA and unrest or economic strain pushes more Cubans to leave by sea.
signposts: US Coast Guard reports of more sea departures
US response on asylum and entry rules
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Migration becomes a bigger US domestic issue and strains neighbouring states.

scenarios.name: Escalation toward force
scenarios.looksLike: Naval action, a blockade-style measure or visible covert operations follow the rhetoric.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: The sharpest Caribbean confrontation in decades, with global reaction and legal criticism.

scenarios.name: Opening or deal
scenarios.looksLike: Havana makes concessions or private talks start, perhaps modelled on how Venezuela's interim arrangement worked.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Lower regional tension, but at the price of a politically messy compromise.

predictions.text: The Cuban government will publicly denounce the appeal as interference, if it has not already (probability about 90%).
The US will announce at least one new Cuba-related sanctions, visa or enforcement measure (probability about 50%).
US forces will not carry out a publicly acknowledged military strike on Cuban territory (probability about 90%).
Cuban leadership will still be in power (probability about 90%).
Reported sea departures from Cuba toward the US will rise noticeably above their autumn 2026 level (probability about 30%; depends on data availability).

actions: Review any Cuba-linked contracts, suppliers or payment routes for sanctions exposure.
Prepare contingency plans for shipping and travel disruption in the Caribbean.
Do not assume Venezuela-style licenses will be offered for Cuba.
Treat Cuba exposure as high political risk until US policy is clearer.
Watch US Treasury and State announcements for sanction changes.
Note that the Venezuela deals show US policy can rewire a country's investment map quickly, but also that they reflect a different situation.
Check government travel advisories before any Cuba trip.
If you send money to family in Cuba, confirm the legal channels are still open before you transfer.
Be sceptical of rumours. Verify announcements with official sources.
Separate public signalling from operational steps, and be clear about what is intended.
Plan for migration and Coast Guard needs in case of an outflow.
Consider the effects on allies in the region, who are watching Venezuela and Cuba closely.

analogues.whatFollowed: A CIA-backed exile landing failed within days, strengthened Castro at home, and pushed Cuba closer to the Soviet Union (background knowledge).
Havana opened the port of Mariel and about 125,000 Cubans reached Florida in a few months, showing how fast Cuban instability can become a US migration issue (background knowledge).

analogues.event: Capture of Maduro and US-backed interim rule in Venezuela
analogues.whatFollowed: Venezuela is now led by acting president Delcy Rodriguez, with US licenses steering oil investment to Western firms. It shows Washington will act, but Cuba differs: no equivalent oil prize is described in our sources.

watch.title: US midterm elections
watch.why: Shows how much the Cuba message plays with voters and may influence how hard the White House pushes afterwards.

watch.title: Havana's response
watch.why: A formal protest, new security measures or arrests would show how Cuba is treating the appeal.

watch.title: New US sanctions or enforcement steps
watch.why: The most likely concrete follow-up if the appeal is more than words.

watch.title: Warship movements
watch.why: Trump said warships could intervene on their return from Iran. Where the ships go matters more than what is said.

watch.title: Coast Guard and migration data
watch.why: Any rise in sea departures would confirm the migration risk flagged in the event summary.

watch.title: Venezuela's oil opening
watch.why: Rodriguez's investment drive and US licenses show whether the regional strategy is delivering stability or just control.

evidence.method: Drafted from three listed articles (Euronews, Al Jazeera, The Guardian, all dated 23 to 24 October 2026), their headlines and summaries, the event summary and the linked Venezuela connection. The Guardian text was truncated, so the warship remark is reported only as far as its standfirst. Historical background is from general knowledge. Effects on Cuba's internal security, sanctions, migration, and all probabilities, are the author's estimates.
